vjimc-2019-cat1-01.title: Quadratic relation and Vieta jumping
vjimc-2019-cat1-01.body:
**The sequence is increasing.** If $a_n\ge1$, then $45a_n^2-36>0$, so $a_{n+1}$ is defined and $2a_{n+1}-7a_n=\sqrt{45a_n^2-36}\ge0$, hence $a_{n+1}\ge\frac72a_n>a_n\ge1$. By induction all $a_n$ are defined, positive and $a_0<a_1<a_2<\cdots$. Also $a_1=\frac{7+3}{2}=5$.

**A quadratic relation.** Squaring $2a_{n+1}-7a_n=\sqrt{45a_n^2-36}$:
$$4a_{n+1}^2-28a_na_{n+1}+49a_n^2=45a_n^2-36\iff a_{n+1}^2-7a_na_{n+1}+a_n^2+9=0.\tag{1}$$

**a)** Fix $n\ge1$. By (1) for $n$ and for $n-1$ (the latter written as $a_{n-1}^2-7a_na_{n-1}+a_n^2+9=0$, since (1) is symmetric in its two variables), both $a_{n+1}$ and $a_{n-1}$ are roots of the quadratic
$$t^2-7a_n\,t+(a_n^2+9)=0 .$$
They are different ($a_{n-1}<a_n<a_{n+1}$), so they are the two roots, and by Vieta's formulas
$$a_{n+1}+a_{n-1}=7a_n,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad a_{n+1}=7a_n-a_{n-1}\quad(n\ge1).$$
Since $a_0=1$ and $a_1=5$ are integers, induction shows that every $a_n$ is an integer, and it is positive by the first paragraph. (The sequence is $1,5,34,233,1597,\dots$)

**b)** By (1), $a_{n+1}^2+a_n^2=7a_na_{n+1}-9$, hence
$$(a_n+a_{n+1})^2=7a_na_{n+1}-9+2a_na_{n+1}=9\,(a_na_{n+1}-1),$$
so
$$a_na_{n+1}-1=\left(\frac{a_n+a_{n+1}}{3}\right)^2 .$$
The left side is an integer and $q=\frac{a_n+a_{n+1}}3$ is rational. A rational number whose square is an integer is itself an integer (if $q=u/v$ in lowest terms with $v>1$, then $u^2/v^2$ is not an integer since $\gcd(u^2,v^2)=1$). Hence $q$ is an integer and $a_na_{n+1}-1=q^2$ is a perfect square. (Examples: $a_1a_2-1=169=13^2$, $a_2a_3-1=7921=89^2$.) ∎

vjimc-2019-cat1-02.title: Common zero vs. a linear relation
vjimc-2019-cat1-02.body:
**a) No.** The three polynomials have a common zero: solving $x+2y+3=0$, $y+z+2=0$, $x+y+z=0$ gives $x=2$, $y=-\frac52$, $z=\frac12$ (check: $2-5+3=0$, $-\frac52+\frac12+2=0$, $2-\frac52+\frac12=0$). Substituting this point into a supposed identity $u^{2019}P+v^{2019}Q+w^{2019}R=2019$ gives $0=2019$, a contradiction. So the triplet is not smart.

**b) Yes.** Now
$$u-v-w=(x+2y+3)-(y+z+2)-(x+y-z)=1 .$$
Let $N=3\cdot2018+1=6055$ and raise this identity to the $N$-th power using the multinomial theorem:
$$1=(u-v-w)^N=\sum_{n_1+n_2+n_3=N}\frac{N!}{n_1!\,n_2!\,n_3!}(-1)^{n_2+n_3}\,u^{n_1}v^{n_2}w^{n_3}.$$
In every term at least one exponent is $\ge2019$: otherwise $n_1+n_2+n_3\le3\cdot2018<N$. Assign each term to one variable whose exponent is $\ge2019$ (say the first such among $u,v,w$) and factor out $u^{2019}$, $v^{2019}$ or $w^{2019}$ respectively. Collecting the terms, we get polynomials $P_0,Q_0,R_0$ (even with integer coefficients) such that
$$u^{2019}P_0+v^{2019}Q_0+w^{2019}R_0=1 .$$
Multiplying by $2019$, the polynomials $P=2019P_0$, $Q=2019Q_0$, $R=2019R_0$ work, so the triplet is smart.

**Answer: a) no, b) yes.** ∎

vjimc-2019-cat1-03.title: Eigenvalues, then signed permutation matrices
vjimc-2019-cat1-03.body:
**Step 1: $M$ must be orthogonal.** A real normal matrix is unitarily diagonalizable: $M=UDU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ (all $\lambda_j\ne0$ since $M$ is invertible). As $M$ is real, $M^T=M^*=U\bar DU^*$, so
$$M_1=(M^T)^{-1}M=U\,\bar D^{-1}D\,U^*=U D_1U^*,\qquad D_1=\operatorname{diag}\big(\lambda_j/\bar\lambda_j\big).$$
$M_1$ is again real and of the same form, so by induction $M_i=UD_iU^*$ where the entries of $D_{i+1}$ are $\mu/\bar\mu$ for the entries $\mu$ of $D_i$. Every number $\mu/\bar\mu$ has modulus $1$, so for $i\ge1$ all diagonal entries of $D_i$ have modulus $1$ and $M_i$ is unitary. Periodicity gives $M=M_0=M_7$, hence $M$ is unitary; being real, it is **orthogonal**: $M^T=M^{-1}$.

**Step 2: the sequence is $M_i=M^{2^i}$.** If $M_i$ is orthogonal, then $(M_i^T)^{-1}=M_i$ and $M_{i+1}=M_i^2$ is orthogonal too. Hence $M_i=M^{2^i}$ for all $i$. The conditions become
- period 7: $M^{2^7}=M$, i.e. (as $M$ is invertible) $M^{127}=I$;
- non-constant: $M_1\ne M_0$, i.e. $M^2\ne M$, i.e. $M\ne I$.

**Step 3: integer orthogonal matrices.** Each column of $M$ is an integer vector of length $1$, so it has exactly one entry $\pm1$ and zeros elsewhere; distinct columns are orthogonal, so the nonzero entries lie in distinct rows. Thus $M$ is a *signed permutation matrix*: $Me_j=\varepsilon_je_{\sigma(j)}$ with $\varepsilon_j=\pm1$ and a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Then $M^k$ is a signed permutation matrix with permutation $\sigma^k$.

**Step 4: lower bound.** From $M^{127}=I$ we get $\sigma^{127}=\mathrm{id}$, so the order of $\sigma$ divides the prime $127$. If $\sigma=\mathrm{id}$, then $M$ is diagonal with entries $\pm1$, so $M^2=I$ and $M=M^{127}(M^2)^{-63}=I$, which is excluded. Hence $\sigma$ has order $127$. The order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths, so $\sigma$ has a cycle of length $127$, forcing $n\ge127$.

**Step 5: construction for $n=127$.** Let $M$ be the permutation matrix of the cycle $e_1\mapsto e_2\mapsto\cdots\mapsto e_{127}\mapsto e_1$. It has integer entries, is orthogonal (hence normal and invertible), and $M_i=M^{2^i}$. Since $M$ has order $127$, $M_i=M_j$ iff $2^i\equiv2^j\pmod{127}$ iff $i\equiv j\pmod 7$ (the order of $2$ modulo $127$ is $7$, as $2^7=128\equiv1$). So the sequence has period exactly $7$ and is non-constant.

(The eigenvalue view: $\lambda\mapsto\lambda/\bar\lambda$ acts as $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^2$ on the unit circle, so period $P$ forces $\lambda^{2^P-1}=1$; for $P=7$, $2^P-1=127$ is prime.)

**Answer: $n=127$.** ∎

vjimc-2019-cat1-04.title: Power series and weighted AM–GM
vjimc-2019-cat1-04.body:
The condition says $\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c=1$; in particular $a,b,c>1$, so $a^a,b^b,c^c>1$.

**Upper bound $K\le18$.** For $a=b=c=3$ the condition holds, the left side equals $3\cdot\frac{27\cdot18}{26^2}=\frac{1458}{676}$ and $\left(\frac{a+b+c}{abc-1}\right)^2=\frac{81}{676}$. So $K\le\frac{1458}{81}=18$.

**The inequality with $K=18$.**

*Step 1: $abc\ge3(a+b+c)$.* By $(x+y+z)^2\ge3(xy+yz+zx)$ with $x=\frac1a,y=\frac1b,z=\frac1c$:
$$1=\Big(\tfrac1a+\tfrac1b+\tfrac1c\Big)^2\ge3\Big(\tfrac1{ab}+\tfrac1{bc}+\tfrac1{ca}\Big)=\frac{3(a+b+c)}{abc}.$$
In particular $abc\ge27>1$.

*Step 2: reduction.* Using $b^2+c^2\ge2bc=\frac{2abc}{a}$ and the analogous bounds,
$$\text{LHS}\ge2abc\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{a^{a-1}}{(a^a-1)^2}.$$
We will show
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{a^{a-1}}{(a^a-1)^2}\ge\frac{abc}{(abc-1)^2}.\tag{$*$}$$
Then, with Step 1,
$$\text{LHS}\ge\frac{2(abc)^2}{(abc-1)^2}\ge\frac{2\cdot9(a+b+c)^2}{(abc-1)^2}=18\left(\frac{a+b+c}{abc-1}\right)^2 .$$

*Step 3: proof of $(*)$.* For $0<x<1$, differentiating $\frac1{1-x}=\sum_{k\ge0}x^k$ gives $\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}=\sum_{k\ge1}kx^k$. With $x=a^{-a}\in(0,1)$:
$$\frac{a^{a-1}}{(a^a-1)^2}=\frac1a\cdot\frac{a^{-a}}{(1-a^{-a})^2}=\frac1a\sum_{k\ge1}k\,a^{-ak}.$$
Hence
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{a^{a-1}}{(a^a-1)^2}=\sum_{k\ge1}k\left(\frac1a\,a^{-ak}+\frac1b\,b^{-bk}+\frac1c\,c^{-ck}\right).$$
Since the weights $\frac1a,\frac1b,\frac1c$ are positive with sum $1$, the weighted AM–GM inequality gives
$$\frac1a\,a^{-ak}+\frac1b\,b^{-bk}+\frac1c\,c^{-ck}\ge\big(a^{-ak}\big)^{1/a}\big(b^{-bk}\big)^{1/b}\big(c^{-ck}\big)^{1/c}=(abc)^{-k}.$$
Therefore the sum is at least $\sum_{k\ge1}k\,(abc)^{-k}=\frac{(abc)^{-1}}{(1-(abc)^{-1})^2}=\frac{abc}{(abc-1)^2}$, which is $(*)$.

Equality throughout requires $a=b=c$, i.e. $a=b=c=3$, where it indeed holds.

**Answer: $K=18$.** ∎
